title: Mapping stalking rates in Queensland: specimen answer
text:
Complete script
# Map recorded stalking incidents per 100,000 residents in Queensland in 2018.

# Load packages
pacman::p_load(here, httr2, sf, sfhotspot, tidyverse)


# Load data --------------------------------------------------------------------

# Download the original data into the workspace
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/qld_stalking.xlsx") |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "qld_stalking.xlsx"))
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/qld_population.csv.gz") |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "qld_population.csv.gz"))
request(
  "https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/qld_police_divisions.gpkg"
) |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "qld_police_divisions.gpkg"))

# Read local data and select stalking counts for 2018
# No need to specify the `sheet` argument in `read_excel()` because the Excel
# file only has one sheet
stalking <- here("data", "raw", "qld_stalking.xlsx") |>
  readxl::read_excel() |>
  filter(year == 2018)
population <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "qld_population.csv.gz"))
divisions <- read_sf(here("data", "raw", "qld_police_divisions.gpkg"))


# Wrangle data -----------------------------------------------------------------

# Join data and calculate rate
stalking_rate <- divisions |>
  left_join(population, by = join_by(division == police_division)) |>
  left_join(stalking, by = join_by(division)) |>
  mutate(rate = stalking / population * 100000)

# Pimpama has no matching population, so its rate remains NA.
# Keep it on the map in grey rather than treating missing data as zero.

# Find divisions with highest stalking rate and label them in order
stalking_rate_highest <- stalking_rate |>
  slice_max(rate, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(desc(rate)) |>
  mutate(label = str_glue("{division} ({scales::ordinal(row_number())})"))


# Create map -------------------------------------------------------------------

stalking_map <- hotspot_map(
  stalking_rate,
  mapping = aes(fill = rate),
  basemap_type = "cartolight",
  caption = str_glue(
    "Map produced by Joe Bloggs on {lubridate::today()}\n",
    "Offences: Queensland Police Service (CC BY 4.0)\n",
    "Population and boundaries: Queensland Government\n",
    "Grey: rate cannot be calculated because population data unavailable"
  ),
  alpha = 0.75,
  linewidth = 0.25
) +
  # Add thicker boundaries for 10 divisions with highest rates
  geom_sf(
    data = stalking_rate_highest,
    colour = "black",
    fill = NA,
    linewidth = 0.75
  ) +
  # Add labels for 10 divisions with highest rates
  geom_sf_label(
    aes(label = str_wrap(label, width = 12)),
    data = stalking_rate_highest,
    alpha = 0.75,
    fill = "white",
    size = 2.5,
    lineheight = 0.95,
    linewidth = 0
  ) +
  scale_fill_distiller(direction = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Recorded stalking rates in Queensland",
    subtitle = str_glue(
      "Ten police divisions with the highest rates are highlighted"
    ),
    fill = "stalking incidents\nper 100,000 people\nin 2018"
  ) +
  theme(
    # Slightly lower the legend in the visual hierarchy by giving it a
    # background that is white and semi-transparent
    legend.background = element_rect(colour = NA, fill = rgb(1, 1, 1, 0.75)),
    # Base legend position on the top-right corner of the legend, which makes
    # moving the legend to the top-right corner easier
    legend.justification = c(1, 1),
    # Add some padding around the legend
    legend.margin = margin(6, 9, 9, 9),
    # Move the legend almost to the top-right corner of the map, since this is
    # the area of the map with no content in it
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(0.95, 0.98),
    # Make the legend title slightly smaller, again reducing its prominence
    legend.title = element_text(size = 10),
    # Left-align the caption
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0),
    # Add some space above and below the plot subtitle
    plot.subtitle = element_text(margin = margin(6, 0, 6, 0)),
    # Make the plot title larger and bold to move it up the visual hierarchy
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16)
  )


# Save map ---------------------------------------------------------------------

# Create map that is 2000px x 2000px
ggsave(
  filename = here("output", "queensland_stalking_rate_map_2018.jpg"),
  plot = stalking_map,
  width = 2000,
  height = 2000,
  units = "px"
)

title: Mapping homicides in the São Paulo region: specimen answer
text:
Complete script
# This script creates a density map of homicides in São Paulo, Brazil, from 2021
# to 2022

# Load packages ----
pacman::p_load(here, httr2, sf, sfhotspot, tidyverse)


# Load data ----

# Download the original data into the workspace
request(
  "https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/sao_paulo_homicides.xlsx"
) |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "sao_paulo_homicides.xlsx"))
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/sao_paulo_muni.geojson") |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "sao_paulo_muni.geojson"))

homicides <- here("data", "raw", "sao_paulo_homicides.xlsx") |>
  # Read Excel file -- there is only one sheet so we won't need to specify
  readxl::read_excel() |>
  # Convert names to snake_case
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  # Keep only homicides in 2021 and 2022
  filter(between(year, 2021, 2022)) |>
  # Convert to an SF object
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = "EPSG:4326") |>
  # Convert to a CRS that uses metres
  st_transform("EPSG:5538")

# Load boundary data
muni <- here("data", "raw", "sao_paulo_muni.geojson") |>
  read_sf() |>
  # Convert names to snake_case
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  # Convert to a CRS that uses metres
  st_transform("EPSG:5538")


# Wrangle data ----

# Create KDE layer
homicides_kde <- homicides |>
  # Estimate density of homicides. São Paulo is very large, so use a larger
  # cell size than for most cities.
  hotspot_kde(
    grid = hotspot_grid(muni, cell_size = 1000, grid_type = "hex"),
    bandwidth_adjust = 0.33,
    quiet = TRUE
  ) |>
  # Clip the density layer to the area for which we have data
  hotspot_clip(muni, quiet = TRUE)


# Map data ----

# Create map
homicide_map <- hotspot_map(
  homicides_kde,
  basemap_type = "cartolight",
  caption = paste0(
    "Homicides: State of São Paulo Public Security Secretariat\n",
    "Boundaries: Institute for Applied Economic Research"
  )
) +
  geom_sf(data = muni, colour = "grey50", fill = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Density of recorded homicides in the São Paulo immediate region",
    subtitle = "Homicides recorded by police, 2021-2022",
    fill = "density of homicides"
  ) +
  # Remove unnecessary map elements
  theme(
    # Put a box around the legend to make it easier to read
    legend.background = element_rect(colour = NA, fill = "grey98"),
    # Since the map is wider than it is tall, change the legend to correspond
    legend.direction = "horizontal",
    # Make the legend expand relative to its top-right corner
    legend.justification = c(1, 1),
    # Add some space around the legend to make it easier to read
    legend.margin = margin(6, 12, 6, 6),
    # Move the legend inside the map area
    legend.position = "inside",
    # Position the legend in the top-right corner of the map
    legend.position.inside = c(0.98, 0.98)
  )

# Save map
ggsave(
  filename = here("output", "sao_paulo_homicide_2021_22.jpg"),
  plot = homicide_map,
  width = 297,
  height = 210,
  units = "mm"
)

title: Mapping fatal shootings in New York City: specimen answer
text:
Complete script
# Map the density of recorded fatal shootings in NYC in 2019,
# excluding Staten Island. Run in the crime_mapping workspace.

## Load packages and data ------------------------------------------------------

# Note: both datasets will be harmonised to use EPSG:6538 for use with
# `hotspot_kde()`

# Load packages
pacman::p_load(ggspatial, here, httr2, sf, sfhotspot, tidyverse)

# Download the original data into the workspace
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/nyc_shootings.csv") |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "nyc_shootings.csv"))
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/nyc_precincts.gpkg") |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "nyc_precincts.gpkg"))

# Read local shootings data and select fatal shootings in 2019
shootings <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "nyc_shootings.csv")) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  filter(murder == TRUE, boro != "STATEN ISLAND") |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = "EPSG:4326") |>
  st_transform("EPSG:6538")

# Load NYC police precincts data
precincts <- here("data", "raw", "nyc_precincts.gpkg") |>
  read_sf() |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  # Filter out precincts in Staten Island, since there are very few fatal
  # shootings there and it takes up a lot of space due to the position of Staten
  # Island relative to the rest of NYC
  filter(precinct <= 119) |>
  st_transform("EPSG:6538")


## Wrangle data ----------------------------------------------------------------

# Calculate KDE
shootings_kde <- shootings |>
  hotspot_kde(
    grid = hotspot_grid(precincts, cell_size = 250),
    bandwidth_adjust = 0.33,
    quiet = TRUE
  ) |>
  hotspot_clip(precincts, quiet = TRUE)


## Make map --------------------------------------------------------------------

shootings_map <- hotspot_map(
  shootings_kde,
  basemap_type = "cartolight",
  caption = str_glue(
    "Author: Joe Bloggs, Date produced: {lubridate::today()}\n",
    "Shootings: New York City Police Department\n",
    "Boundaries: City of New York (CC BY 3.0 AU)"
  )
) +
  geom_sf(data = precincts, colour = "grey33", fill = NA) +
  geom_sf_label(
    aes(label = scales::ordinal(precinct)),
    data = precincts,
    alpha = 0.5,
    colour = "grey33",
    fill = "white",
    size = 2.5,
    linewidth = NA
  ) +
  annotation_scale(width_hint = 1 / 5, style = "ticks", location = "br") +
  labs(
    title = str_glue(
      "Density of recorded fatal shootings in New York City"
    ),
    subtitle = str_glue(
      "Fatal shootings recorded by NYC Police, 2019, excluding Staten Island"
    ),
    fill = "density of\nshootings"
  ) +
  # Make the map square (i.e. have an aspect or height/width ratio of 1) to
  # expand the area covered by the map without reducing the size of the area
  # covered by the data layer
  fixed_plot_aspect(ratio = 1) +
  theme(
    # We're going to overlay the legend on the map, so we should give the
    # legend a solid background
    legend.background = element_rect(colour = NA, fill = "#F2F2F2"),
    # Use the top-right corner of the legend as the anchor point for determining
    # its position
    legend.justification = c(1, 1),
    # Make the legend colour bar smaller
    legend.key.width = unit(0.8, "lines"),
    # Create a margin around the legend, since it has a solid background
    legend.margin = margin(6, 6, 6, 6),
    # Move the top-right corner of the legend to be very near the top-right
    # corner of the map
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(0.98, 0.98),
    # Make the legend and title smaller to reduce their visual prominence
    legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.7)),
    legend.title = element_text(size = rel(0.8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = rel(0.8), margin = margin(3, 0, 6, 0)),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey45", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0)
  )


# Save the finished map in the workspace output folder
ggsave(
  here("output", "nyc_fatal_shootings_2019.png"),
  plot = shootings_map,
  width = 210,
  height = 210,
  units = "mm"
)

section: Why the code is organised this way
text:
Why the code is organised this way
There are two points about this script that are worth noting. The first is that the map does not show all of New York City. The code deliberately filters out Staten Island, which has very few fatal shootings but would otherwise occupy a large proportion of the map because it is so geographically large. Staten Island is excluded to make the map easier to read, particularly since readers of crime analysis products such as crime maps are usually (although not always) interested in the areas with most crime.
The second feature is that the map legend has been moved inside the map area using various arguments to the theme() function. This means the legend doesn’t take up space on the page/screen that can usefully be used to show the data. Look through the comments in the code to understand how this was done. The theme() function is very flexible and allows you to change the position of the legend, the size of the text, the background colour and many other features. You can also use theme() to change the appearance of other map elements such as the title, subtitle and caption.

Complete script
# Map recorded damage to property (méfait) in Montreal in 2025.

# Load the packages needed for downloading, preparing and mapping the data
pacman::p_load(here, httr2, sf, sfhotspot, tidyverse)

# Download the original compressed CSV file and keep a local copy
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/montreal_mefait.csv.gz") |>
  # Save the file in the workspace's data/raw folder
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "montreal_mefait.csv.gz"))

# Locate the downloaded file within the workspace
mefait_2025 <- here("data", "raw", "montreal_mefait.csv.gz") |>
  # Read the compressed CSV file, including its date column
  read_csv() |>
  # Convert column names to snake_case
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  # Keep dates from 1 January to 31 December 2025 inclusive
  filter(date >= ymd("2025-01-01"), date <= ymd("2025-12-31")) |>
  # Interpret x and y as projected coordinates in metres using EPSG:2950
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = "EPSG:2950")

# Draw a point map over a base map, with small, partly transparent points
hotspot_map(
  mefait_2025,
  basemap_type = "cartolight",
  alpha = 0.25,
  colour = "blue2",
  size = 0.5
)

title: Mapping damage to property in Montreal: specimen answer
section: Why this code is organised this way
text:
Why this code is organised this way
Load packages first. R can only use functions from packages that are loaded. The easiest way to load packages is to load them all at the very start of a script, so that it’s easy to see at a glance all the packages that a particular script needs. That means that, for example, if you are writing a later part of a long R script and you want to use a function from a particular package, it is easy to go to the start of the code and see whether that package is already loaded or whether you need to load it.
Download, then read. The request() and req_perform() functions from the httr2 package save the original CSV file into the data/raw directory so that you have a local copy of the original, unwrangled data. That means that if you later make a mistake in wrangling the data, you can always go back to the original dataset. Note that read_csv() can handle compressed versions of CSV files, including the .csv.gz file downloaded here.
Filter by date. The download contains incidents from 2016 to 2025 inclusive. read_csv() recognises the date column as dates. The two conditions in filter() keep dates on or after 1 January 2025 and on or before 31 December 2025, therefore including every day of 2025. ymd() converts the text values (e.g. "2025-12-31") to dates. Every row already relates to méfait, so we do not need to filter by crime type.
Describe the original coordinates. st_as_sf() uses the x and y columns to locate each incident. The argument crs = "EPSG:2950" tells R how to interpret those coordinates. They are eastings and northings in metres, rather than longitude and latitude as in some of the other exercises. Note that assigning a coordinate reference system using st_as_sf() describes the existing coordinates – it does not transform the coordinates into a different system (for which we would use st_transform()).
Finish with the map. hotspot_map() plots mefait_2025 over a base map. Small, partly transparent blue points help show overlapping incidents against the light background.

# This script produces a dot map of thefts from vehicles in Vancouver in 2020

# Load packages

  "https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/vancouver_thefts.csv.gz"

  thefts_from_vehicles,
  basemap_type = "cartodark",
  alpha = 0.25,
  colour = "orange3",
  size = 0.5
)

# Map recorded fatal terrorist attacks in London from 2010 to 2018.

# Load packages

attacks <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "london_attacks.csv"))

attacks_sf <- st_as_sf(

  crs = "EPSG:4326"
)

# Transform to a projected coordinate reference system suitable for London
attacks_sf_trans <- st_transform(attacks_sf, crs = "EPSG:27700")

# Display the map
hotspot_map(
  attacks_sf_trans,
  basemap_type = "cartolight",
  colour = "red2",
  size = 5
)

In this exercise you will practise downloading and reading data, data wrangling, kernel density estimation, clipping datasets, adding multiple layers to a map, specifying map labels and saving a map to a file.

What your map should show
Your map should show homicides in the immediate region (IR) of São Paulo, Brazil, between 2021 and 2022 based on data from the Public Security Secretariat (SSP) of the State of São Paulo. You can download the data from:
https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/sao_paulo_homicides.xlsx
The homicide dataset documentation explains that homicides with missing coordinates have been removed. Your map therefore shows only homicides with recorded locations. The file covers 2017–2022, so filter it to keep only 2021 and 2022.
The co-ordinate reference system you need to use for this dataset is EPSG:4326.
Your map should include:

a layer showing the density of homicides in the São Paulo region,
a suitable base map,
layers showing the boundaries of municipalities in the region,
a suitable declarative title and descriptive subtitle,
a suitable caption acknowledging the sources of the data (including the base map),
a suitable legend.

You can download municipality boundaries – provided by IPEA (the Institute for Applied Economic Research) – from:
https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/sao_paulo_muni.geojson
See the municipality boundary documentation for the columns and source. These boundaries are from 2010, while the homicides you are mapping are from 2021–2022.
This dataset uses the SIRGAS 2000 co-ordinate reference system, EPSG:4674, which measures distances in decimal degrees.
The two datasets use different co-ordinate reference systems, both of which measure distances in decimal degrees. You will need to convert both datasets to a suitable CRS that measures distances in metres. EPSG:5538 would be a suitable code for this area of Brazil.
Every step of your code should be accompanied by an explanatory comment (on one or more lines starting with a # symbol and a space). Your code should only produce and save a map (and possibly some R messages or warnings), not output anything else (e.g. a copy of the data).
The code should save the finished map as a JPEG image with a .jpg file extension in the output folder of your project. The map should be saved at A4 size.


Checklist for this exercise
Make sure you have checked that your map and code meet all of the following requirements.

The map

The map shows the density of crimes.
The density layer is clipped to the area for which you have data.
The cell size and bandwidth of the density layer make it easy to see concentrations of crime.
The map shows only homicides in 2021 and 2022.
The map shows the boundary of each municipality.
The base map does not distract from the data layer or make it harder to see the data layer.
There is a declarative title and a descriptive subtitle.
The caption acknowledges the data sources where required.
You have made design choices that make it as easy as possible to show where homicides are most concentrated.
You have made design choices that make sure the municipality boundaries do not obscure the places with the highest concentrations of crime.



The code

There is no temporary code – e.g. head() or install.packages() – in your script file.
The code loads all the necessary packages at the start of the script.
The code downloads the data file from the URL to a temporary file and then loads it.
The code converts all the column names in the data to snake_case and only uses snake-case object names.
The code converts the data to an SF object.
The code transforms the data to a suitable co-ordinate reference system.
The code filters the data to only include the period of time you are interested in.
Every step of your code is accompanied by an explanatory comment.

title: Mapping stalking rates in Queensland
text: For this exercise, you must create the code needed to make a map of stalking incidents in the state of Queensland, Australia, in 2018.

title: Mapping stalking rates in Queensland
text:
Before you start
Complete Chapters 1–9 of Learn Crime Mapping with R.
In this exercise you will practise downloading and reading data, data wrangling, combining multiple datasets and calculating rates, creating a choropleth map, and saving a map to a file.

title: Mapping stalking rates in Queensland
text:
What your map must show
Your map must show the incidence rate of stalking incidents in 2018 in each police division in Queensland. You will need three datasets to produce this map:
Stalking counts for each division in Excel format: https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/qld_stalking.xlsx
Population data for each division in CSV format: https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/qld_population.csv.gz
Police division boundaries in geopackage format: https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/qld_police_divisions.gpkg
See the documentation for the stalking counts, population and police division boundaries for the columns and sources. The population figures are from 2016 and the boundaries are from 2022, while you are mapping offences from 2018. Your rates therefore use an earlier population count rather than the population in 2018. Acknowledge the Queensland Police Service for the offence counts and the Queensland Government for the boundaries, following the attribution licences listed in the documentation.
Your map must include:

a layer showing the rate of stalking crimes in each division,
a suitable base map,
the contextual information (title etc.) needed to help readers understand the map properly.

If you want to make this exercise slightly more challenging, add a layer showing the names of the 10 divisions with the highest stalking rates.
Every step of your code should be accompanied by an explanatory comment (on one or more lines starting with a # symbol and a space). Your code should only produce and save a map (and possibly some R messages or warnings), not output anything else (e.g. a copy of the data).
Your code should include the code needed to save your map in JPEG format, 2,000 pixels on each side.

title: Mapping property crime rates in Poland
text: For this exercise, you must create a script containing the code needed to make an interactive map of property offences in counties (powiats) in Poland in 2023.

title: Mapping property crime rates in Poland
text:
Before you start
Complete Chapters 1–9 of Learn Crime Mapping with R.
In this exercise you will practise downloading and reading data, data wrangling, selecting records for one year, combining datasets, calculating rates and creating an interactive choropleth map using leaflet.

title: Mapping property crime rates in Poland
text:
What your map must show
Your map must show the incidence rate of property offences per 100,000 residents in 2023 in each powiat (county) in Poland. You will need three datasets to produce this map:
Property offence counts for each powiat in Excel format: https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/poland_property_crime_counts.xlsx
Population data for each powiat in tab-separated (TSV) format: https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/poland_population.tsv
Powiat boundaries in geopackage format: https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/poland_powiat_boundaries.gpkg
See the documentation for the property offence counts, population and powiat boundaries for the columns and sources. The offence and population counts cover 2022–24: select only records where rok (year) is 2023. The offence counts relate to completed preparatory proceedings; the population is measured on 31 December 2023. The boundaries come from the 2025 archive. Acknowledge Statistics Poland (CC BY 4.0) and GUGiK/PRG as described in the documentation.
Your map must include:

a layer showing the incidence rate of property offences in each powiat,
a suitable base map,
the contextual information (title etc.) needed to help readers understand the map properly.

Your map should use the leaflet functions introduced in Chapter 9 of the textbook, including a legend, labels showing each powiat’s name and rate, and an inset map.
Every step of your code should be accompanied by an explanatory comment (on one or more lines starting with a # symbol and a space). Your code should only produce a map (and possibly some R messages or warnings), not output anything else (e.g. a copy of the data).
Leave the leaflet stack unassigned so that running it in the R Console displays the map directly. Do not store the map in an object or save it as an HTML file.

text:

The map acknowledges Statistics Poland (CC BY 4.0) and GUGiK/PRG as the data sources.
You have made design choices that make it as easy as possible to show where the property crime rate is highest.
You have made design choices that make sure the boundaries do not obscure the places with the highest rates of crime.

There is no temporary code – e.g. head() or install.packages() – in your script file.
The code loads all the necessary packages at the start of the script.
The code downloads the data file from the URL to a local file and then loads it.

The code selects 2023 only from both statistical datasets, joins the datasets correctly and calculates offences per 100,000 residents.

The leaflet stack displays the map directly without storing it in an object or saving it as an HTML file.
